questions.q: Written amid the gloom of the pandemic, the editorial points to something seen every morning. What lesson does it take from the sunrise?
options: The world moves from darkness towards light; one state gives way to a brighter one, so there is no cause for despair
Yes. “Remove the word ‘hopelessness’ from your dictionary.”
Nature is indifferent to human trouble
Not quite. The article says: The world moves from darkness towards light; one state gives way to a brighter one, so there is no cause for despair.
The day is short and must be hurried through
Not quite. The article says: The world moves from darkness towards light; one state gives way to a brighter one, so there is no cause for despair.
Only the early riser succeeds
Not quite. The article says: The world moves from darkness towards light; one state gives way to a brighter one, so there is no cause for despair.
questions.rationale: “There is a system in place in this world which brings light after darkness. Human beings are no exception to this principle.”

questions.q: Which verse of the Quran does the editorial quote as glad tidings of hope?
options: “The life of this world is but play”
Not quite. The article says: “Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor is He displeased with you” (93:3).
“Every soul shall taste death”
Not quite. The article says: “Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor is He displeased with you” (93:3).
“Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor is He displeased with you” (93:3)
Right. Hardship is a reminder to turn back, not abandonment.
“Man was created weak”
Not quite. The article says: “Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor is He displeased with you” (93:3).
questions.rationale: “The Creator gives us glad tidings of hope in the Quran: ‘Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor is He displeased with you.’ (93: 3)”

questions.q: What does the Quran (49:6) instruct when news is brought to you?
options: Verify it fully before acting on it or passing it on, lest you harm others unknowingly
Well read. And regret it afterwards.
Believe it if many are repeating it
Not quite. The article says: Verify it fully before acting on it or passing it on, lest you harm others unknowingly.
Share it quickly so others are warned
Not quite. The article says: Verify it fully before acting on it or passing it on, lest you harm others unknowingly.
Ignore all news entirely
Not quite. The article says: Verify it fully before acting on it or passing it on, lest you harm others unknowingly.
questions.rationale: “Believers, if an evil-doer brings you news, ascertain the correctness of the report fully, lest you unwittingly harm others, and then regret what you have done.”

questions.q: According to the Hadith quoted, what is “enough lying for a man”?
options: To break a promise
Not quite. The article says: To pass on everything he hears.
To exaggerate his own deeds
Not quite. The article says: To pass on everything he hears.
To pass on everything he hears
Yes. One need not invent a lie to spread one.
To keep silent about the truth
Not quite. The article says: To pass on everything he hears.
questions.rationale: “It is enough lying for a man to speak of everything that he hears.”

questions.q: Trains now carry a “fog-safe device.” What does the article call the mind’s equivalent amid a flood of information?
options: Following the most popular opinion
Not quite. The article says: The trained ability to set aside the irrelevant and keep only what bears on the matter.
The trained ability to set aside the irrelevant and keep only what bears on the matter
Well reasoned. The principle of elimination.
Reading as much as possible
Not quite. The article says: The trained ability to set aside the irrelevant and keep only what bears on the matter.
Avoiding the internet altogether
Not quite. The article says: The trained ability to set aside the irrelevant and keep only what bears on the matter.
questions.rationale: “This device is an internally prepared mind trained in the art of differentiation… This technique can be called the principle of elimination.”

questions.q: In the story, a hunter spends his life cutting steps up a mountain in search of the Bird of Truth and dies without reaching it. What comforts him at the end?
options: A feather falls beside him, and he knows others will climb by the steps he cut
Right. “They will find truth and through me.”
He catches the bird at last
Not quite. The article says: A feather falls beside him, and he knows others will climb by the steps he cut.
He is carried down by friends
Not quite. The article says: A feather falls beside him, and he knows others will climb by the steps he cut.
He learns the bird never existed
Not quite. The article says: A feather falls beside him, and he knows others will climb by the steps he cut.
questions.rationale: “Where I lie down, worn out, other men will stand young and fresh. By the steps that I have cut they will climb.”

questions.q: “Everyone is a seeker… But few are finders.” What reason does the article give?
options: Finders are chosen by birth
Not quite. The article says: Seeking is instinctive, but finding comes only through one’s own conscious effort.
Seeking is instinctive, but finding comes only through one’s own conscious effort
Correct. With an open mind and humility before truth.
Truth is hidden from most people
Not quite. The article says: Seeking is instinctive, but finding comes only through one’s own conscious effort.
Seeking stops in adulthood
Not quite. The article says: Seeking is instinctive, but finding comes only through one’s own conscious effort.
questions.rationale: “Where seeking is instinctive, finding is the outcome of one’s own conscious effort.”

questions.q: Which of these marks a true seeker, according to the article?
options: He looks at the truth itself, not at the standing of the person who presents it
Yes. Truth always comes through a human being.
He waits for the majority to decide
Not quite. The article says: He looks at the truth itself, not at the standing of the person who presents it.
He trusts only what is impressive
Not quite. The article says: He looks at the truth itself, not at the standing of the person who presents it.
He accepts only what his elders taught
Not quite. The article says: He looks at the truth itself, not at the standing of the person who presents it.
questions.rationale: “A true seeker looks not at the person who presents the truth but at the truth itself.”

questions.q: Truth accords with human nature, yet people often refuse it. What does the article say holds them back?
options: Lack of intelligence
Not quite. The article says: Psychological barriers – fear for their way of life or status, or prejudice against the one presenting it.
Psychological barriers – fear for their way of life or status, or prejudice against the one presenting it
Exactly. A little honest thought would remove them.
Lack of time
Not quite. The article says: Psychological barriers – fear for their way of life or status, or prejudice against the one presenting it.
Lack of books
Not quite. The article says: Psychological barriers – fear for their way of life or status, or prejudice against the one presenting it.
questions.rationale: “They are psychologically inhibited from doing so. Acceptance of the truth might disrupt their materialistic life-pattern. They might have to lower their worldly status.”

questions.q: How does the commentary ask us to regard the losses and troubles that come in life?
options: As accidents with no meaning
Not quite. The article says: As messages meant to wake us to reflection, not as mere ups and downs.
As messages meant to wake us to reflection, not as mere ups and downs
Well read. To dismiss them dulls the conscience.
As other people’s fault
Not quite. The article says: As messages meant to wake us to reflection, not as mere ups and downs.
As signs that effort is useless
Not quite. The article says: As messages meant to wake us to reflection, not as mere ups and downs.
questions.rationale: “Life’s events are not mere happenings but vibrant messages from God sent to wake a man up from his sleep of forgetfulness.”
